transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-01
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Lina Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood CSM), Dana Ortiz (Blueforge Head DS), Elliot Park (Blueforge Sec Lead), Samir Rao (Blueforge Platform), Jules Moreno (Blueforge PM)

Summary (auto):
- Kickoff to scope privacy-first pilot focusing on prompt storage, PII redaction, retention windows, and workload benchmark sizing.
- Agreed artifacts: redaction rules, retention matrix, sample dataset, benchmark harness and timeline.
- Success criteria: PII redaction >=95% on test set, 95th pct latency <300ms for short prompts, throughput target 10-15 req/s sustained for canonical flow, no unredacted logs stored longer than configured retention.

Topics: pilot scope; telemetry & logs; ephemeral vs persisted prompts; benchmark plan; timeline; security requirements (SOC2, KMS)

Action items captured in metadata above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lina: alright everyone thanks for joining, um we'll do a brief agenda — scope, success criteria, samples and then timings. Marcus'll cover the benchmark plan.
[00:34] Dana: great thanks Lina. A few context points from our side — Blueforge runs user support automation, 3M monthly convs, peak burst to 150 reqs/sec for short prompts, but canonical would be 8-12 reqs per second for our pilot traffic. We're sensitive to any PII leaking into logs.
[01:12] Marcus: quick clarifying question, when you say "PII" can you scope what counts for you? is it names, emails, acc numbers, or also free-form health info?
[01:27] Dana: good q — it's names, email, phone, national id, credit tokens, also some sensitive free-text like patient notes — though pilot excludes PHI-heavy flows. We want to validate redaction on the front-end and at ingestion so not stored in plain text.
[01:48] Elliot: and from security we need assurance on retention windows, we can't keep prompt text beyond the retention policy. Ideally ephemeral storage for prompts, with ability to optionally persist a redacted copy.
[02:11] Lina: great that's the privacy-first constraint. For pilot we can support two modes: ephemeral-only (no prompt persisted) or ephemeral + redacted persistence. We'll prototype both and run benchmarks.
[02:33] Samir: what does ephemeral mean operationally? is it never written to disk or is it encrypted at rest and rotated?
[02:44] Marcus: good point — our private deployment supports in-memory KV cache for ephemerality, and we can set prompt retention to zero in logs. For hosted we'd route to ephemeral only unless you opt-in. Under the hood we do write transient traces to allow debugging but those can be scrubbed and auto-deleted within the retention policy you configure. sometimes the transcript will show a temp trace id.
[03:12] Jules: can you talk about the redaction approach? simple regex or model-based?
[03:20] Marcus: we use a hybrid: deterministic rules (regex, canonical patterns) for high-precision items like SSNs, emails; plus an optional NER model to catch freeform PII. The NER improves recall but introduces occasional false positives which we tune. For the pilot we suggest starting with deterministic + model scan in a non-blocking pass and then move to blocking redaction once recall is acceptable.
[03:56] Dana: ok that seems sensible. how do you measure recall & precision?
[04:05] Marcus: benchmark harness will run labeled sample sets and report metrics: PII recall, precision, percent unredacted tokens, and false redact rate. We'll aim for >=95% recall on the labeled pilot set and <2% false redact for customer conversational data.
[04:28] Elliot: from compliance we also need KMS integration and audit logs for decryption events.
[04:36] Priya: noted, we have KMS integrations for major cloud providers and can provide HSM/KMS integration docs. We'll include the audit log pattern — who, when, reason for decryption.
[04:52] Samir: what's the benchmark workload look like?
[04:58] Marcus: here's the plan — two passes. (1) Functional redaction test using 10k labeled samples (we ask Blueforge to supply anonymized set) and (2) performance bench: synthetic replay of representative traffic with same token distribution and seq lengths. For perf we plan a 2-hour run at target concurrency bands: steady 10 req/s, burst tests to 100 req/s for 1 minute, and long tail runs to 8k token sequences to check memory/kvcache and OOM behavior.
[05:36] Lina: can you map that to success criteria we can agree on today?
[05:41] Marcus: yeah tentatively: redaction recall >=95% on labeled set; precision >=98% for deterministic items; 95th percentile end-to-end latency <300ms for short prompts (<128 tokens) under sustained 10-15 req/s; no persisted unredacted prompts beyond retention window; and CPU/GPU memory within acceptable bounds (no OOMs during 2 hour run).
[06:08] Dana: for us the risk tolerance is low on leakage; if the redaction isn't hitting 95% we can't go to production. Also cost will be a factor — what's the billing model for the pilot?
[06:21] Lina: pilot is typically usage-based with a capped budget we agree on; we can also provide discounted reserved capacity for the bench. We'll follow-up with a pricing note after we scope exact load.
[06:35] Elliot: also need to validate the console telemetry: per-request tokens, cost, model version, and a redaction stamp for persisted items so we can audit redactions.
[06:50] Marcus: yep console will surface token counts, per-route latency and a redaction status flag (redacted/partially-redacted/raw). We'll make sure those fields appear in the pilot telemetry export.
[07:07] Jules: timeline? how long to get a bench running once we share samples?
[07:12] Marcus: typical turnaround: 3-5 business days to prepare harness and synthetic loader once we have the sample data; then schedule the 2-hour run (preferably in your low-traffic maintenance window). After the run, 2 business days to analyze results and produce a summary.
[07:32] Dana: so roughly two weeks end-to-end from samples to readout?
[07:36] Lina: that matches our expectation — sample by 7/8, bench 7/13 window, readout by 7/20.
[07:45] Elliot: legal question — can we avoid transfer of raw PII to Redwood infra for this pilot? We could provide redaction or pseudonymization before transfer.
[07:58] Priya: yes we support both options. If you want zero raw transfer, you can run a local pre-redaction step and send only hashed or redacted text; we'll run the model and benchmark on that. This affects redaction metric quality since you won't have ground truth raw; for the labeled set we recommend providing token-level labels but with anonymized identifiers.
[08:19] Samir: in terms of deployment mode — are you recommending hosted or dedicated for this pilot?
[08:25] Marcus: for initial pilot hosted is faster; for stricter isolation we can spin up a dedicated pool (reserved) which gives you control plane separation and VPC peering. Dedicated takes more lead time (typically a week to provision) but provides better determinism for latency and tenancy.
[08:45] Dana: we might need dedicated for internal security requirements but for proof-of-concept hosted would be fine if we can ensure ephemeral-only mode.
[08:54] Marcus: understood. We'll plan for hosted ephemeral first, with a parallel plan to validate dedicated if needed.
[09:03] Jules: what about model variants & quantization — will redaction behave differently across models?
[09:10] Marcus: generally redaction is upstream of generation so behavior is consistent, but tokenization boundaries and model context can change NER behavior. We'll run redaction tests across the model variants you plan to use. Quantized variants may have slightly different latency and memory profiles; we'll call that out in the bench.
[09:32] Dana: can we get a checklist of required artifacts we need to give you?
[09:37] Lina: yes — we'll send a Kickoff packet. Key items: (1) labeled sample set (10k rows) or a subset, (2) production traffic profile (requests/sec, token distribution, seq length percentiles), (3) retention policy and legal boundaries, (4) list of sensitive entity types to prioritize, (5) maintenance window preferences for bench run, (6) security contacts and network info if you want VPC/dedicated.
[10:05] Elliot: on retention windows — we need flexibility: 0 days (ephemeral), 7 days, 30 days for different teams. Can you set per-tenant retention?
[10:18] Marcus: yes retention is per-tenant and per-route. We'll document the config options. For ephemeral we set logs retention to 0 and scrub KV caches after completion. There might be short-lived debug traces but those can be configured to auto-delete within a minute.
[10:36] Samir: during the bench how do you handle debug logging if we hit a failure we need traces for debugging?
[10:43] Marcus: we generate ephemeral traces with trace IDs and can create a secure, time-limited retrieval link for you. Access to traces is governed by RBAC and KMS.
[10:54] Dana: what's the expected artifact you'll provide after bench?
[10:58] Marcus: a bench report: redaction metrics (precision/recall), latency percentiles, token-level cost estimate, memory/CPU telemetry, and notes for any items needing follow-up. We'll also include a CSV with per-sample results for the labeled set.
[11:15] Jules: great. Any constraints on the sample data format?
[11:19] Lina: CSV or JSONL accepted. If you send JSONL, please include fields: id, prompt, expected_redacted_prompt(optional), labels(optional). We'll sanitize on receipt and store per agreed retention settings.
[11:34] Elliot: one more compliance ask: we need the redaction rules documented so audit can sign off; can you provide that?
[11:40] Priya: yes we'll share a redaction rules doc + an architecture diagram showing how prompts flow through our pipeline, which services touch the data, and how KMS is used.
[11:50] Samir: who will be our point of contact at Redwood for the bench window?
[11:54] Lina: primary is Marcus for SE work, I'll coordinate commercial and scheduling. Priya will help with onboarding and security docs.
[12:02] Dana: good — let's recap next steps.
[12:07] Lina: recap: Redwood sends kickoff packet and redaction rules (due 7/6). Blueforge sends sample set and traffic profile (due 7/8). Marcus builds harness (due 7/10), bench run week of 7/13, readout 7/20. Decision point: go/no-go for expanded pilot based on redaction and latency metrics.
[12:28] Jules: ok thanks all.
[12:30] (meeting ends)
